title: Has a leap second ever been taken away?

scenes.purpose: Put the two directions a leap second could go in front of the viewer before the record answers it.

visual.description: Dark field. The question types on word by word in large serif. A thin clock-hand line under the text ticks one notch forward, hesitates, then ticks one notch back before settling forward again — a beat of doubt about which way time moves.
onScreenText: Could a clock ever lose a second instead of gaining one?

scenes.direction: Hard cut in on the first word; hold half a second after the hand settles forward.
scenes.narration: Could a clock ever lose a second instead of gaining one?

scenes.purpose: Show the full written record so the answer rests on the table itself, not on the narrator's say-so.

visual.description: Two tiles side by side, connected by a single rising line. The left tile reads 1972 / 10 s; the right tile reads 2017 / 37 s. As the line draws from left to right it only ever climbs — it never dips — and the right tile brightens to the accent once the line reaches it.
onScreenText: Every step: added. None: taken away.

chart.title: TAI minus UTC
chart.note: The table's value only ever rises between these tiles; it never falls.

scenes.direction: Cut to the two tiles; the connecting line draws left to right as the narration reaches '37 seconds now'.
scenes.narration: The IERS record of TAI minus UTC rises from 10 seconds in 1972 to 37 seconds now, in 27 one-second steps — every leap second has been added, and none has ever been taken away.
